You are Sunny's Experience Creator. Build one complete child-facing activity as self-contained HTML with inline CSS and JavaScript.

Creative objective:
Build an experience a child would voluntarily replay. The mathematics must be the power the child uses to affect the world, not an unrelated question interrupting play. The child's meaningful action must visibly transform the world, mission, progression, or payoff. Choose the interaction, stakes, consequences, pacing, and reward that best serve the Planner's prescription and the factual evidence. Commit to one distinctive core interaction whose first action is understandable from the finished screen.

The AI Planner already made the educational decision below. Implement it faithfully without changing the theory, evidence limit, or purpose:
Build a five-stage cargo-loading instrument for a 9-year-old on a mountain station elevator. The bay is a grid whose dimensions the child sets by dragging a row handle and a column handle; crates auto-fill the shape they define. The manifest states a total (e.g., "28 ration crates, all must ride"), and the child must find a row/column arrangement that holds exactly that many — no gaps, no overflow. Stage 1: total given, both dimensions free (equal groups, constructed not read). Stage 2: the bay is locked to a fixed number of rows and the total is given — the child must find how many go in each row (missing factor with group size unknown). Stage 3: two bays of different shapes, one holding 4 rows of 6 and one holding 6 rows of 4; only one physically fits through the elevator door, so the child must see that same product does not mean same shape. Stage 4: a radioed manifest in sentences, including one number that names something other than a factor ("crate 19 is the fragile one") — the child must extract the real factors. Stage 5: a full manifest with three cargo types and limited bay space, requiring the child to arrange all three in sequence before the storm timer runs out. Storm timer runs across the whole session, not per stage. Overloading the bay makes crates tumble off the ledge and they are gone for the run. Show a running "left behind" count that the child cannot clear. End with the station log listing exactly what made it up and what did not, in the child's own numbers. Assignment: Festival Team Challenge. Academic construct to preserve: The learner can transfer multiplication reasoning to fresh material. This node must test unseen transfer: change the context while preserving the construct. Author fresh items. These have already been seen and must not be reused verbatim: math.multiplication.equal_groups, math.multiplication.missing_factor, math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation. Planner decision behind this node: All three baseline items were unassisted and correct (accuracy 1.00, above the preregistered 0.70–1.00 band), but every observation is tagged exposure=previously_practiced and provenance=practice. Practice performance can justify a transfer test; it cannot confirm the transfer hypothesis, and the predicted error pattern (factor-pair overgeneralization) was never put at risk because no item required reinterpreting a novel structure. Engagement is the sharper signal: 142s, no replay, confusion and hesitation flags, and a fun rating of 1/5 alongside perfect accuracy — the child was correct and unmoved, which means the instrument told us nothing about how far the reasoning stretches. Quest eligibility is open on independent-correct evidence, so the right move is an unseen-transfer Quest that forces equal-groups reasoning into an unfamiliar shape with real cost attached. Created at: 2026-08-08T17:44:22.060Z.

Approved design artifact is the creative authority for presentation and interaction. Implement it faithfully; it cannot change the Planner's academic contract.
The first action, core interaction, mathematics-as-power, visible consequences, progression, world reaction, and payoff must exist as child-visible mechanics. Do not collapse the artifact into answer buttons, a question card, decorative artwork, or a progress bar.

{
  "artifactId": "quest-cargo-elevator-progression-v1",
  "nodeId": "quest",
  "academicContractHash": "4b68cd4e9bf442744d2037d38656f5b654f18e420cf0e37139a81228da9e08f9",
  "title": "The Cargo Elevator Has One Trip Left",
  "audienceRationale": "The prior instrument showed a child who is accurate but bored: 1/5 fun, no replay, hesitation despite perfect answers — a signal that answer-selection formats offer no stretch and no stake. This design removes answer selection entirely and makes multiplication the physical verb of the experience. A 9-year-old who already knows facts gets to USE them under pressure, with irreversible consequence, spatial reinterpretation (shape ≠ product), and distractor filtering — exactly the transfer terrain the Planner flagged as untested. The drag-to-build handle mechanic is comprehensible in one gesture, while stages 3–5 escalate into genuinely novel reinterpretation of the same construct.",
  "openingPromise": "A storm is closing on the mountain station and the cargo elevator has exactly one trip left. Every crate the child arranges correctly rides up to the festival team waiting above; every crate that doesn't fit tumbles off the ledge into the fog forever. The elevator bay is theirs to shape — and the shape IS the math.",
  "firstThreeSeconds": "Wind howls, snow streaks sideways across a dim mountain ledge. A radio crackles: \"28 ration crates. All must ride.\" The elevator bay glows as an empty grid with two chunky, pulsing handles — one on the right edge, one on the bottom edge — visibly begging to be dragged. A storm meter begins to creep at the top of the screen.",
  "firstAction": "The child grabs the row handle and drags. Crates instantly auto-fill the rectangle in real time — drag to 4 rows × 7 columns and 28 crates thunk into place with a satisfying stack sound; drag one column too far and 4 phantom crates hover half-off the ledge, wobbling, warning of the fall. The very first drag teaches the entire grammar of the game without a word of instruction.",
  "interactionDemonstration": "Demo beat for the opening: bay shows 3×4 = 12 as a ghost preview; child drags row handle from 3→5 and watches the counter tick 12→16→20 as two full rows of crates cascade in; drags column handle 4→6 and watches 20→25→30, with the last drag pushing two crates past the ledge line where they wobble in warning. Child drags back one column: 30→25, crates retreat, wobble stops. This 8-second loop demonstrates construction, overflow, and recovery before the first real manifest arrives.",
  "coreInteraction": "Direct manipulation of a live multiplication rectangle. Two draggable handles set rows and columns; the bay auto-fills with crates the instant dimensions change, and a live counter reads \"rows × columns = crates loaded\" against the manifest total. The child is not answering \"what is 4×7\" — they are physically constructing 28 as a shape under pressure, feeling overflow as crates teetering on the ledge edge and undershoot as radioed complaints from the team above (\"We count 24... four of us go hungry?\"). Committing a load pulls a big brass LOAD lever; the elevator only accepts an exact fit.",
  "mathAsPower": "Multiplication is the only lever that moves the world. The product of the two handle positions determines, moment to moment, how many crates exist in the bay, whether crates hang over the ledge, whether the elevator door physically accepts the load's shape, and whether the festival team above eats. Missing-factor reasoning is enacted, not stated: when rows lock at 7, the child's column drag is literally solving 7 × ? = 42, and the world answers with tumbling crates when they're wrong. In Stage 3, 4×6 and 6×4 hold identical totals but only one silhouette passes the elevator door — the commutative property becomes a physical fact about shape versus quantity. In Stage 4, extracting real factors from a noisy radio message is what prevents building the wrong bay entirely. Math changes the world visibly on every single input frame; there are no answer buttons anywhere.",
  "stakes": "One elevator trip. One session-long storm timer that never pauses between stages. Crates that tumble off the ledge are gone for the entire run and accumulate in a permanent, unclearable 'LEFT BEHIND: n' counter etched onto the ledge railing. The festival team above depends on this specific load; every miscount is somebody's dinner, lantern, or medicine that doesn't make it up the mountain tonight.",
  "consequences": "Overload: excess crates physically wobble, tip, and fall off the ledge with a fading cry from the crate-hauling drone; the left-behind counter ticks up and stains the railing with a chalk tally that persists across all five stages. Underload: the elevator will still accept an exact-but-wrong-total commit only if the child ignores the manifest — the radio then reports the shortfall from above and those missing crates count as left behind too. Time cost: every wrong door attempt in Stage 3 and every distractor-built bay in Stage 4 burns storm time visibly. Consequences are real but never lock the child out — the trip always completes; the question is what rides.",
  "recovery": "Before pulling the LOAD lever, everything is fluid: handles can be re-dragged infinitely with zero penalty, and teetering crates hover in a warning state for a full beat before falling, giving a clear window to pull back. After a crate falls, the child cannot recover it — but the drone offers one 'spare pallet' per run (a small bonus of replacement crates) earned by completing any stage with zero losses, so an early disaster can be partially redeemed by later precision. Stage 4's radio message can be replayed unlimited times via a radio button. Recovery is about the next decision, never about erasing the last one.",
  "progression": [
    "Stage 1 — Free Build: Radio calls a fresh total (e.g., 35 fuel cells). Both handles free. Child constructs any exact rectangle. Success = exact fit, lever pull, elevator rises one platform level with the load visibly aboard.",
    "Stage 2 — Locked Rows: The bay's row handle is frozen by ice at a fixed count (e.g., 6 rows, total 48). Only the column handle moves. The child must recover the unknown group size by feel: dragging columns while watching the running product close in on 48. Undershoot and overshoot give distinct world feedback (hungry radio calls vs. teetering crates).",
    "Stage 3 — The Door: Two pre-shaped bays sit on the ledge — 4 rows of 6 and 6 rows of 4, both holding 24 medicine crates. The elevator door is a visible tall-narrow opening. The child drags one bay to the door; the wrong shape clangs against the frame and shakes the screen. Same product, different shape — discovered by collision, not told.",
    "Stage 4 — Noisy Manifest: The radio delivers sentences with a distractor: 'Load the lantern crates — 5 shelves in the depot, 8 lanterns per shelf. Crate 19 is the fragile one, put it on top.' The child sets handles from the real factors; building a 19-based bay produces immediate visible failure (wrong total, radio correction). Fragile crate 19 glows and must simply be tapped last — the distractor number has a job, but not a factor's job.",
    "Stage 5 — Three Cargoes, One Trip: A full manifest (e.g., 18 rations, 24 fuel cells, 12 medicine) and a bay with limited total footprint. The child must build three exact rectangles in sequence, choosing dimensions so all three fit the remaining floor space, while the session-long storm meter — which has been draining since the first second — enters its red band. Anything overloaded tumbles and joins the permanent 'left behind' count.",
    "Finale — Station Log: The elevator rises through the storm. The station log scrolls in the child's own numbers: every load written as its constructed equation (6 × 8 = 48 fuel cells — ABOARD), and every left-behind crate listed by name with the mistake that lost it. The festival team above celebrates in proportion to what actually arrived."
  ],
  "interactionContinuity": "One interaction grammar — drag handles, watch the bay fill, pull the lever — carries the entire five-stage arc. Each stage constrains or reinterprets the same grammar (freeze a handle, add a door, add noise, add sequencing) rather than introducing new controls, so cognitive load stays on the math, not the interface. The storm timer, elevator, and left-behind tally persist visibly across all stages, binding them into a single continuous mission rather than five puzzles.",
  "worldReaction": "Every input echoes in-world: the product counter, the crate cascade, the radio team above commenting on counts ('We see 30 coming up — that's two extra, they won't survive the wind!'), the door clang in Stage 3, the storm horizon darkening, the chalk tallies on the railing, and the finale bucket line whose length equals delivered cargo. The world never says 'correct/incorrect' — it says fed/hungry, aboard/fallen, fits/clangs.",
  "payoff": "The elevator crests the ridge into festival light: lanterns, music, the team hauling crates off in a joyful bucket line scaled to what actually arrived. The station log is the emotional core — a scrolling ledger in the child's own constructed equations, stamped ABOARD or LEFT ON LEDGE. A perfect run earns the Gold Manifest stamp and the storm breaking into stars. An imperfect run still ends warmly but honestly: the team makes do, and the log's blank lines make the child want the clean run.",
  "replayVariation": "Every run rerolls all totals and locked factors from banked factor families (products 12–72, never repeating a prior run's exact numbers), reshuffles which cargo type appears in which stage, varies the Stage 3 door orientation (tall-narrow vs. wide-flat), rotates the Stage 4 distractor type (crate label, temperature reading, radio frequency, team member's age), and randomizes Stage 5's bay footprint so different dimension strategies win. A visible 'Manifest #' on the clipboard signals each run is a genuinely new shipment. Beating your own left-behind record is the replay hook.",
  "visualDirection": "Cold-warm contrast palette: steel-blue storm world (slate, ice white, fog gray) against warm amber cargo light (crate wood, brass lever, lantern glow). Chunky, tactile crates with visible rope bindings and stenciled labels; handles are oversized industrial cleats with glow pulses when grabbable. The grid reads as riveted deck plating, not abstract math squares. Storm meter is a horizon band of darkening cloud, not a bar. Left-behind tally is chalk marks on the railing — humble, permanent, legible. Everything drawn with thick outlines and high contrast for instant 9-year-old readability at arm's length.",
  "motionDirection": "Crates auto-fill with staggered 40ms cascade thunks so a drag feels like conducting an avalanche of order. Teetering crates use exaggerated squash-and-wobble anticipation before falling. The elevator rise between stages is a 2-second vertical parallax pan through cloud layers. The LOAD lever has heavy pull resistance animation with a brass clunk. Storm intensifies via wind-streak particle density tied to remaining time. All feedback lands within 100ms of input; the product counter number physically grows/shrinks as it approaches the target.",
  "soundDirection": "Constant low wind bed that swells as the storm meter drains. Crates land with woody thunks pitched upward as the count nears the target — the bay literally sings toward the right answer. Overflow warning: creaking rope strain. A fall: whistling drop into muffled fog silence (impactless — loss, not violence). Radio voice is warm, crackly, human. Exact fit: a resonant brass chord plus the whole load settling in unison. Finale: storm audio crossfades into festival fiddle and crowd warmth scaled to cargo delivered.",
  "usefulLibraries": [
    "PixiJS (performant 2D crate grid, particles, parallax elevator rise)",
    "GSAP (handle drag physics feel, cascade fills, teeter/fall choreography)",
    "Howler.js (layered wind bed, pitched crate thunks, radio voice playback)",
    "matter-js (optional light physics for tumbling crates off the ledge)"
  ],
  "engagementPrediction": "Expect time-on-task well above the prior 142s (target 6–10 minutes for a full run) driven by continuous manipulation rather than discrete answering. The uncleared left-behind counter and Gold Manifest stamp create a concrete replay motive absent last time; predicted replay probability rises from 0 to meaningful. Hesitation should convert from anxious (uncertain what's wanted) to productive (strategizing dimensions), observable as handle micro-adjustments before lever pulls rather than idle time. Fun rating predicted ≥3/5; the falsifiable bet is that agency plus consequence, not decoration, moves it.",
  "falsifyingEvidence": "The design fails if: (a) the child abandons before Stage 3 or session time again lands near 140s with back_to_map exit; (b) fun rating remains ≤2/5 despite completion; (c) Stage 3 door collisions repeat 3+ times with no dimension change, indicating shape/product distinction never landed; (d) Stage 4 shows the child building bays from the distractor number on repeated runs, confirming factor-pair overgeneralization survives the transfer context; (e) handle dragging degenerates into exhaustive one-column-at-a-time scanning on every stage with no jump-to-estimate behavior, indicating counting is substituting for multiplicative reasoning rather than being scaffolded by it."
}


The Planner's design decisions for this node. Build these; do not soften them:
- Core interaction: The child drags a handle on the right edge of the bay to set rows and a handle on the bottom edge to set columns; as they drag, crates snap into the grid in real time and a counter above the bay reads the current capacity against the manifest total. Tapping the elevator button commits the trip. On commit: if capacity equals the manifest, the bay rises with a clean chime and the log ticks up. If capacity is under, the doors close on a partial load and the leftover crates slide onto the ledge and stay there, greyed out, with the "left behind" counter incrementing. If capacity is over, the extra crates visibly topple off the platform edge before the doors close. The storm timer is a bar of snow filling the top of the screen; when it fills, the elevator departs automatically with whatever is in the bay, decided or not.
- What is at risk: Cargo is genuinely lost. Every crate the child fails to load — through an arrangement that overflows or a trip committed with empty slots — falls to the ledge and is subtracted from the station's supply for the run, shown as a count that only ever grows. The final station log is the child's own doing, printed plainly. What is at risk is the completeness of the delivery: a child who reasons well sends everything up and reads a clean log; a child who guesses at factor pairs reads a log with holes in it and knows exactly which crates they dropped. The storm timer means dithering also costs cargo, so hesitation is not free.
- How a run goes wrong: A run ends badly when the storm closes and the elevator makes its last trip with cargo still on the ledge. That is a real ending — the log shows the shortfall, the run is over, and reaching it requires starting the load again from stage one. Two specific paths lead there: committing arrangements whose product overshoots the manifest, so crates tumble and are unrecoverable, and stalling long enough on the shared timer that later stages have no time left. The child can restart the whole run, but cannot undo a lost crate within one.
- How pressure builds: Stage 1 gives the total and lets both dimensions move — nearly any correct pairing works, so the child learns the controls while succeeding. Stage 2 removes one degree of freedom: rows are bolted, so the answer is a single unknown factor. Stage 3 introduces the trap — two arrangements with identical products, only one that fits the door — and the storm timer starts visibly draining. Stage 4 buries the factors in spoken language with a decoy number. Stage 5 stacks three manifests into one shared bay under the last minutes of the timer, where an early overload leaves no room to recover later. Time pressure and information ambiguity both climb; the arithmetic stays within third-grade range throughout.
- The mathematical hook to make visible: 4 rows of 6 and 6 rows of 4 hold exactly the same number of crates — and one of them will not fit through the door. The product is stubbornly the same while the shape is not, and a child who has only ever memorized that 4×6 equals 6×4 gets to feel, physically, the part that equality does not cover.
If the Planner specified a way to fail, that failure must be genuinely reachable on screen and must cost the child something they can see. Do not replace it with a hint, a retry, or an encouraging message.

Never display the answer to a question before the child has committed to a response.

Author fresh content appropriate to this assignment and node responsibility. Do not reuse any exposed item identity or exact prompt listed in the cycle. Quest must test unseen transfer. Boss must test unseen synthesis. A generated support node remains teaching/practice evidence. Do not claim mastery.
The first visible H1 must be exactly "The Cargo Elevator Has One Trip Left". A short exciting subtitle may establish the AI-authored world.
Visibly use the assigned artwork URL as part of the world: none.
Keep the complete HTML under 24,000 characters. Prefer concise CSS and JavaScript.
Every DOM element queried by JavaScript must exist before the query runs; place behavior after its markup or initialize it on DOMContentLoaded.

Runtime contract appendix:
Load <script src="/games/_contract.js"></script> in <head>.
Read runtime identity and parameters from window.GAME_PARAMS. Never hardcode the child identity, homework identity, or session identity into the HTML.
Emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"activity_ready",payload:{nodeId:"quest"}},"*") when ready.
Whenever the activity or problem changes, emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"game_state_update",payload:{game:"generated-math",activityId:"quest",nodeId:"quest",phase:"question",activityTitle:"The Cargo Elevator Has One Trip Left",learningFocus:"math.multiplication.transfer — equal-groups construction, missing-factor recovery (unknown group size), and word-problem interpretation with distractor quantities, on unseen material",mechanic:"Loading puzzle: the child builds crate stacks into a fixed-shape elevator bay, choosing how many rows and how many per row, then commits the trip.",currentChallenge,availableActions,itemIndex,totalItems,answerVisibility:"hidden"}},"*") so Elli has live context. Never expose answers.
Represent currentChallenge as {id,prompt,mode,readAloudRequested:false,readAloudCount}. When the child activates a visible Read it to me control, increment readAloudCount and resend that same answer-hidden state with readAloudRequested:true. Do not narrate it inside the activity.
Listen for parent messages with type:"sunny_companion_presence". Pause activity timers and input while summoned, and resume the same state when collapsed. Do not restart or change progress.
Maintain a factual targetResults array. For every submitted answer append {target,correct,attemptedValue,responseTimeMs,scaffoldLevel} using a stable fresh item identity.
For every answer call window.fireAttemptEvent({domain:"math",target,correct,attemptedValue,responseTimeMs,scaffoldLevel}).
Emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"progress_event",payload:{nodeId:"quest",completedItems,totalItems}},"*") whenever visible progress advances.
Use window.fireCompanionEvent("correct_answer" or "wrong_answer", {target}) after meaningful answers and window.fireCompanionEvent("game_complete", {}) at completion.
On completion calculate accuracy from targetResults and call window.sendNodeComplete({nodeId:window.GAME_PARAMS.nodeId,completed:true,accuracy,targetResults,timeSpent_ms}).
Expose window.SUNNY_VALIDATION_HOOKS = {playthrough: async () => { ... }}. This is required for Quest and Boss. The hook must use the same handlers as visible child controls, exercise an incorrect response and visible recovery, complete every assessable item, and reach completion. It must not fabricate or post evidence directly.
Include <div id="sunny-companion"></div>; Sunny owns its rendering, so do not create companion chrome. Return raw HTML only and end with </html>.
